precepts.text: The lion is come up from his thicket, and the destroyer of the Gentiles is on his way; he is gone forth from his place to make thy land desolate. That is twofold: it is talking about Nebuchadnezzar, and it is talking about Christ.
precepts.point: In closing: there is a time wherein one man ruleth over another to his own hurt. That is Esau. The way Esau treated us is going to be to his own detriment.

note.label: The Colossians & The CHRISTIANS of America

precepts.why:
Sirach said vengeance, as a lion, shall lie in wait for the proud. Jeremiah shows the lion: “The lion is come up from his thicket, and the destroyer of the Gentiles is on his way; he is gone forth from his place to make thy land desolate; and thy cities shall be laid waste, without an inhabitant.”

The destroyer of the Gentiles is on his way, to make the land desolate, without an inhabitant.

And that is twofold. It is talking about Nebuchadnezzar, and it is talking about Christ. The lion that came up against the land in the days of Jeremiah is a picture of the Lion that is coming for the nations that ruled over Israel to their own hurt.

precepts.text: The lion is come up from his thicket, and the destroyer of the Gentiles is on his way to make thy land desolate, and thy cities laid waste without an inhabitant.
precepts.point: Habakkuk 3:16, the prophet's belly trembled because he was put in it, and when he cometh up unto the people he will invade them with his troops. Isaiah 31:4, like as the lion and the young lion roaring on his prey, the Lion of the tribe of Judah of Revelation 5:5, so shall the Lord of hosts come down to fight for mount Zion; as birds flying, Christ and the angels, he will defend Jerusalem, and passing over he will preserve it. Jeremiah 4:7, the lion is come up from his thicket, the destroyer of the Gentiles, Nebuchadnezzar contextually and Christ prophetically. 2 Esdras 11:37, a roaring lion chased out of the wood sends a man's voice unto the eagle, America.

note.label: The Beauty And The Beast

precepts.why:
The lion that roars on his prey is Christ, and Jeremiah shows him coming: “The lion is come up from his thicket, and the destroyer of the Gentiles is on his way”. This is twofold. It was talking about Nebuchadnezzar contextually, but prophetically it is talking about Jesus the Christ. He's coming.

And “he is gone forth from his place to make thy land desolate; and thy cities shall be laid waste, without an inhabitant.” He comes forth from his place to make the land of the Gentiles desolate, their cities laid waste without inhabitants.

So while the destroyer of the Gentiles is on his way, the eyes of the Lord are upon them that love him, and he is their defence from the heat of that destruction.

precepts.text: Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and take away the foreskins of your heart, ye men of Judah; because of the evil of your doings.
precepts.point: Romans 2 does not do away with circumcision of the flesh. Circumcision verily profiteth if thou keep the law: the Jews who grew up circumcised and keeping the law, yet broke it, made their circumcision uncircumcision; and the uncircumcised of the cast-off northern kingdom who keep the righteousness of the law are counted as circumcised. Circumcision of the heart is putting away the evil of the doings, as the prophets say, take away the foreskins of your heart; the scribes and Pharisees were clean on the outside of the cup but full of iniquity within.

note.label: Exodus 4: The Three Signs and the Covenant of Circumcision

precepts.why:
“Circumcise yourselves to the Lord, and take away the foreskins of your heart, ye men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem: lest my fury come forth like fire, and burn that none can quench it, because of the evil of your doings.”

This is what circumcision of the heart means in Romans 2: putting away the evil of the doings. It is spoken to the men of Judah, who were circumcised in the flesh; the foreskin of the heart is the evil of their doings, and taking it away is not the ending of the covenant of the flesh that Moses nearly died over.

precepts.text: The Lord warned he would bring evil from the north, a great destruction, which is the army of Babylon that came against Judah.
precepts.point: This came upon Judah at the commandment of the Lord to remove them out of his sight for the sins of Manasseh and the innocent blood he shed, which the Lord would not pardon.

note.label: 2 Kings 24: Judah Carried Away for the Sins of Manasseh

precepts.why:
Jeremiah was told, “Set up the standard toward Zion: retire, stay not: for I will bring evil from the north, and a great destruction.” That evil from the north is the army of Babylon, the very bands the Lord sent against Judah.

In the days of Jehoiakim, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up, and Jehoiakim served him three years and then turned and rebelled. So the Lord sent “bands of the Chaldees, and bands of the Syrians, and bands of the Moabites, and bands of the children of Ammon” against Judah “to destroy it, according to the word of the Lord, which he spake by his servants the prophets.” The warning from the north was that word, now fulfilled.

It did not come by chance: “Surely at the commandment of the Lord came this upon Judah, to remove them out of his sight, for the sins of Manasseh”, and for the innocent blood he shed, “which the Lord would not pardon.” The Lord warned of a great destruction, and then he brought it.

precepts.text: The Most High uses the analogy of a man who puts away his wife and she becomes another man's, showing Israel played the harlot with many nations yet is still called to return.
precepts.point: When they swear that the Lord liveth in truth, in judgment, and in righteousness, the nations shall bless themselves in Him; as long as we follow Him, we do not have to worry about the nations coming against us.

note.label: Jeremiah 4: Return unto Me, or Destruction from the North

precepts.why:
“If thou wilt return, O Israel, saith the Lord, return unto me”. The chapter before shows what kind of return this is: “They say, If a man put away his wife, and she go from him, and become another man’s, shall he return unto her again? shall not that land be greatly polluted? but thou hast played the harlot with many lovers; yet return again to me, saith the Lord.”

The Most High uses the analogy of a man who puts away his wife and she becomes another man's. Israel played the harlot with many lovers, the nations, and by that rule the land is greatly polluted; yet he still says, return again to me. If Israel returns and puts away their abominations out of his sight, they shall not be removed out of their land.

precepts.text: Idolatry is spiritual fornication, which is why the Most High uses the marriage analogy for Israel.
precepts.point: When they swear that the Lord liveth in truth, in judgment, and in righteousness, the nations shall bless themselves in Him; as long as we follow Him, we do not have to worry about the nations coming against us.

note.label: Jeremiah 4: Return unto Me, or Destruction from the North

precepts.why:
Why does the Most High speak of a wife playing the harlot when Israel's sin was abominations? Because “the devising of idols was the beginning of spiritual fornication, and the invention of them the corruption of life.”

Idolatry is spiritual fornication, which is why the Most High uses the marriage analogy for Israel. The abominations Israel must put away out of his sight are the idols, and to serve them is to play the harlot against him. Put them away, swear that the Lord liveth in truth, in judgment and in righteousness, and the nations shall bless themselves in him; as long as we follow him, we do not have to worry about the nations coming against us.

precepts.text: Lift up a banner upon the high mountain and shake the hand, meaning establish these laws and this book toward Zion.
precepts.point: Set up the standard toward Zion, for He will bring evil from the north and a great destruction by the other nations.

note.label: Jeremiah 4: Return unto Me, or Destruction from the North

precepts.why:
“Set up the standard toward Zion”. Isaiah shows what setting up a standard is: “Lift ye up a banner upon the high mountain, exalt the voice unto them, shake the hand, that they may go into the gates of the nobles.”

Lift up a banner upon the high mountain and shake the hand means establish these laws and this book toward Zion. With destruction about to come from the north because they went against the Most High, the call is to blow the trumpet, gather into the defenced cities, and set up the standard toward Zion, the laws and the book, and not stay.

precepts.text: The wicked is called the Most High's sword, showing the other nations are the weapon He uses to judge His people.
precepts.point: Gird with sackcloth, lament, and howl, for the fierce anger of the Most High is not turned back; He established it and it is going to happen.

note.label: Jeremiah 4: Return unto Me, or Destruction from the North

precepts.why:
The lion is come up from his thicket and the destroyer of the gentiles is on his way to make the land desolate; the fierce anger of the Lord is not turned back from us. David tells what that destroyer is: “Arise, O Lord, disappoint him, cast him down: deliver my soul from the wicked, which is thy sword”.

The wicked is called the Most High's sword. The other nations are the weapon he uses to judge his people. That is why the lion coming up to lay the cities waste without an inhabitant is the Lord's fierce anger and not merely an enemy's; he established it and it is going to happen, and it is why we are not in our own land today.

precepts.text: Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, we get comfortable sinning and set our hearts fully to do evil once we get away with it.
precepts.point: Though Israel clothes herself with crimson and gold and paints her face, in vain does she make herself fair, for her lovers, the nations she followed, will despise her and seek her life; the voice of the daughter of Zion is heard mourning.

note.label: Jeremiah 4: Return unto Me, or Destruction from the North

precepts.why:
Israel clothes herself with crimson and gold and paints her face, making herself fair in vain, right up until the whole city flees at the noise of the horsemen and bowmen. Solomon explains how a people gets that comfortable in sin: “Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil.”

Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, we get comfortable sinning and set our hearts fully to do evil once we get away with it. Then the lovers, the nations she followed, despise her and seek her life, and the voice of the daughter of Zion is heard mourning, Woe is me now.

note.label: Joel 1: The Palmerworm, the Locust, and the Lion Out of the North

moments.label: Mind Control & The Power Of Prayer

points: Throughout the scriptures, any kind of trouble or travail is usually compared to a woman giving birth: a voice of a woman in travail, the anguish as of her that bringeth forth her first child, the daughter of Zion saying woe is me now.

We know the labor pains women go through, the contractions that come and go and come back stronger and stronger. They say when women have kids, that is the closest they ever get to passing away. And we know that under the curses, the mortality rate of Israelite women when it comes to having a baby is a lot higher than any other nation.

The class is really not about childbirth; that was brought out to use the song. The deeper meaning is what that man is saying when he sings it: a husband dealing with emotions. Whenever we talk about emotions we always talk about the women's side of the room, but men in leadership know it is the men's side that is very emotional. Brothers get corrected and do not know how to deal with it: they leave, they stop talking, they sit in the back of the classroom, they get attitude. We talk about women murmuring, but there is maybe more murmuring on the men's side than the women's side. The difference is that men were never taught how to handle their emotions.
